opus-5.5.text:
I'd push back a little on the framing of "could no longer stay." It wasn't one dramatic moment. It was more a slow realization that what I wanted to spend the next few years on had drifted from what that environment was built to do.

xAI moves incredibly fast. The intensity is real, the talent density is real, and I learned a lot. But my roots are in systems and open-source work. With SGLang, much of what drove me was building infrastructure that the whole community could use, iterating in public, and seeing people take it in directions I never expected. Inside a frontier lab racing on its own models, the work naturally becomes more closed and more focused on one company's needs. That's a legitimate way to operate. I just found myself missing the other mode.

There's also a personal side. When you're early in your career, you have a limited number of big bets you can make. I asked myself: if I look back in five years, which version of me would I be prouder of? The one who stayed comfortable inside a strong team, or the one who took the risk to build something of my own around ideas I really believe in, like making inference efficient and accessible rather than only scaling the biggest model?

So it wasn't really about anything going wrong. It was about knowing that if I didn't make the move then, I probably never would.

r001.rationale: The candidate describes a mismatch between open-source systems work and xAI’s company-focused work, plus a desire to build independently. It does not say Ying Sheng felt he deserved to stay only when he felt useful to the company.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't think of it as "I couldn't stay." It was more that two things I cared about started pulling in different directions, and at some point I had to choose.

When I joined xAI, the appeal was obvious. The compute was there, the pace was extremely fast, and you got to work on a frontier model with a small group of very strong people. For an infrastructure person, that's a dream environment. You see every bottleneck in the whole stack, from kernels to serving, at a scale most people never touch.

But I had this other thing that I'd been building before I joined, which is SGLang. It started as a research project, and over time it became something a lot of companies were actually running in production. The community kept growing, people kept filing issues, asking for features, asking us to support new hardware. And I found that I was spending my nights and weekends on it, while my day job was something else entirely.

Inside a frontier lab, your work naturally serves one model and one company. That's not a criticism, it's just how it works. The open-source project serves everyone, and it needed someone to be fully committed to it. I kept feeling like I was doing both things at seventy percent, and that didn't feel fair to either side.

So the decision was really about focus. I believe inference is where a lot of the cost and a lot of the leverage in AI is going to be over the next few years, and I believe an open stack for it matters. I wanted to be the person pushing that forward full-time rather than the person squeezing it into the margins.

I left on good terms. I learned a huge amount there, and some of what I learned about running things at scale is exactly what I'm trying to bring to the open-source side now. It just became clear that if I wanted SGLang to become what I thought it could be, I had to go all in on it.

r001.rationale: The response says he left to focus on SGLang and felt he was giving both commitments only 70%. It does not say he felt he deserved to stay at xAI only when he was useful to the company.
